1) 执行 curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats: 1) Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/jvm?pretty and compare the growth of old collection_count and collection_time_in_millis; 2) Start with the heap alert path: lower pipeline.batch.size and check stateful filters; 3) Run jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -30 to see the object distribution; when abnormal it is usually a build-up of event objects; 4) After tuning, confirm the old GC rate falls; if it does not, split the pipeline or scale Logstash horizontally.

1) Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/jvm?pretty to confirm heap_used_percent and GC counts; 2) The most common trigger is an oversized pipeline.batch.size; estimate memory as batch.size x worker count x average event size and lower it; 3) Check for filters that cache large amounts of state in memory (aggregate, ruby) and cap their cache size; 4) Only once the configuration is sane should you raise -Xmx in jvm.options, generally staying under half of physical memory and under 8 GB.

1) Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty and compare duration_in_millis across plugins to find the biggest contributor; 2) If the time is concentrated in an output, investigate the downstream first (Elasticsearch write rejection rate, bulk queue); when the downstream is the root cause, fix it there rather than in Logstash; 3) If it is concentrated in filters, focus on grok: replace complex regexes with dissect or add anchors to avoid catastrophic backtracking; 4) If the host CPU is already saturated, raising pipeline.workers will not help and you need to scale out.

1) Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty to find the pipeline and plugin burning the most CPU; 2) Capture stacks with jstack <pid>; many threads inside regex methods point to grok overhead; 3) If it is still high after tuning filters, check whether pipeline.workers exceeds the real CPU core count and is causing context-switch overhead; 4) If the host is genuinely at its limit, scale out and spread the load at the collection layer.

1) Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty to find the pipeline whose events.out is not increasing; 2) For that pipeline, look at the per-plugin event breakdown; the blockage is usually in an output (Elasticsearch rejecting writes, Kafka unreachable); 3) Check logstash-plain.log for retry/backoff errors and confirm whether the downstream is returning 429 or timing out; 4) After the downstream recovers, watch events.out come back; if it stays flat, restart Logstash and check whether the persistent queue is corrupted.

1) Run curl -s localhost:9600/_node/stats/pipelines?pretty and sort plugins by duration_in_millis to find the slow one; 2) Slow grok is the usual cause: load-test with --config.debug on a small sample and replace broad regexes with dissect; 3) Filters that make external lookups (jdbc_streaming, elasticsearch, dns) must have caching enabled and timeouts set; 4) After tuning, re-run the same sample set and compare duration to confirm the improvement is real.
